system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2155-04-17 11:36:00 to 2155-04-21 17:34:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type 1 diabetes, and a history of coronary artery disease and Chagas disease was admitted with a three-day history of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and subjective fever. He was evaluated for possible cardiac or gastrointestinal causes, but ECG and cardiac enzymes were stable, and imaging showed no evidence of pancreatitis or abscess. CT and chest X-ray revealed small bilateral pleural effusions and trace abdominal fluid consistent with volume overload. Stool studies were negative for bacterial and parasitic infections, supporting a diagnosis of viral gastroenteritis. His symptoms improved with supportive care, and he underwent scheduled hemodialysis. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to monitor weight, continue heart failure and diabetes medications, and follow up on abnormal labs showing transient leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated creatine kinase.
problems: Intestinal infection due to other organism, not elsewhere classified
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease
Diabetes with renal manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled
Diabetes with ophthalmic manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled
Chagas' disease without mention of organ involvement
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft
Other nonspecific findings on examination of blood

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ man with epigastric pain.  Evaluate for infiltrate.

COMPARISON:  Multiple chest radiographs, most recent of ___.

FRONTAL AND LATERAL VIEWS OF THE CHEST:  There is pleural thickening
bilaterally, more prominent on the right.  There is a small pleural effusion,
also on the right, and possibly smaller one on the left, similar in appearance
to the prior study.  Moderate cardiomegaly is unchanged.  There are no focal
areas of consolidation.  There is no free air beneath the diaphragms.  Patient
is status post CABG with intact midline sternotomy wires.

IMPRESSION:  Small bilateral pleural effusions, stable.  Stable cardiomegaly.

HISTORY:  ___ male with severe epigastric abdominal pain.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were generated through the abdomen and pelvis after
administration of 130 cc of Optiray intravenous contrast.  Coronal and
sagittal reconstructions were performed.

COMPARISON:  ___.

CT ABDOMEN WITH IV CONTRAST:  In the visualized portion of the chest, there
are small bilateral pleural effusions, right greater than left, and have
improved from previous study.

The liver shows no focal lesion or biliary dilatation.  Gallbladder shows 
trace wall edema without pericholecystic fluid or marked distention.  There is
one small gallstone within the gallbladder.  The spleen is normal in size and
appearance.  Pancreas is diminutive and shows no masses, cysts, or
calcifications. There is trace fat-stranding about the tail of the pancreas.
No focal fluid collections are seen. The pancreas enhances homogeneously. The
adrenal glands are normal appearing bilaterally.  The kidneys enhance with and
excrete contrast symmetrically, although they both appear mildly atrophic. 
The small and large intestine show no evidence of obstruction or wall
thickening.  The aorta, IVC, portal vein, and their major branches all appear
patent.  There is no evidence of aortic aneurysmal dilatation or dissection. 
No lymphadenopathy or free air. A trace amount of free fluid is noted about
the liver and within the right anterior pararenal space.

CT PELVIS WITH IV CONTRAST:  The bladder is unremarkable.  The rectum and
prostate appear unremarkable. No pelvic free fluid.

BONES:  No lytic or sclerotic lesions are seen.  Mild degenerative changes are
noted in the lumbar spine.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No evidence of aortic dissection or abdominal aortic aneurysm.
2.  Trace fat-stranding about the tail of the pancreas. Given the patient's
elevated lipase, this finding is compatible with acute pancreatitis. No focal
fluid collections.
3.  Cholelithiasis without evidence of acute cholecystitis. Trace gallbladder
wall edema is likely secondary to acute pancreatitis.
4.  Small bilateral pleural effusion.

CHEST RADIOGRAPH

INDICATION:  Pancreatitis, rule out pneumonia or pleural effusion.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  As compared to the previous radiograph, today's upright AP
radiograph confirms the presence of mild right-sided pleural effusion.  On the
left, no effusion is seen.  Unchanged status post sternotomy with unchanged
appearance of the cardiac silhouette.  No hilar or mediastinal changes.  No
focal parenchymal opacity suggesting pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, doctor. I had sharp pain in my upper belly yesterday afternoon after eating a sandwich. It went through to my back and got worse overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you vomit or have any diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I threw up twice and had one episode of watery diarrhea. Even the air on my skin hurt yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds very uncomfortable. We checked your labs and found your potassium was quite high, at 6.8. That can be dangerous for your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: High potassium? But I’m on dialysis. That’s never happened before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s unusual, but pancreatitis can sometimes cause it. Your EKG showed bradycardia—your heart rate dropped to 41—and some changes that we think were due to the high potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my heart okay? I’ve had heart issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your heart is stable now. The cardiology team reviewed it and believes the changes were from the potassium. Your heart rate improved after treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the belly pain? Could it be pancreatitis again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan shows some inflammation in the tail of the pancreas, and your lipase is elevated. That confirms acute pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. What caused it this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure. You have gallstones, but no signs of infection. It might be related to your pancreatic anatomy. We’ll keep you on clear liquids for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before. It’s awful. Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Most cases improve with rest, fluids, and pain control. We’ll monitor you closely and advance your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished your dialysis session. Your potassium dropped to 5.8, and we’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I felt shaky earlier. Was that from the potassium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We gave you calcium and insulin to bring it down quickly. You’re responding well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative, so no infection was found. That supports pancreatitis as the main issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. We only use them if there’s clear evidence of infection, which we don’t have.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your lipase went up to 231 last night but is now coming down to 146. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll start you on a clear liquid diet today and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray today shows the right pleural effusion is still mild. The left side has cleared. It’s stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Inflammation can cause fluid to collect. But it’s small and not causing breathing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your pain is much better, and your labs are improving. We’re going to advance your diet to soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hoping for discharge tomorrow. We want to make sure you can eat without pain and your potassium stays normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my diabetes? I was low last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose dropped to 56. We gave you juice and adjusted your insulin. You’re back on your regular Lantus dose now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to be careful with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll make sure your sliding scale is clear for home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news. Your lipase is down to 139 and potassium is 4.1. Your heart rate is stable at 64.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll do one more set of labs in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I’ll need to watch my diet, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Avoid fatty or fried foods. Stick to small, frequent meals. And keep taking your omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge labs are back. Potassium is 3.9, creatinine 7.7, lipase 67. All improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What meds am I taking home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual ones—Lantus, captopril, carvedilol, omeprazole, aspirin, and the others. Plus, a short supply of oral Dilaudid for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long should I take the Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only as needed. Try to reduce it over the next few days. If pain returns, call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your regular M-W-F schedule. Stay hydrated and monitor your weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If my weight goes up more than 3 pounds, I should call?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That could mean fluid buildup. Also watch for shortness of breath or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad this is over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Stay safe and keep up with your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your nephrologist and primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, and a history of pancreatitis presented with acute epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting after eating. He was found to have hyperkalemia with associated bradycardia and EKG changes, which resolved with medical treatment and hemodialysis. Imaging confirmed acute pancreatitis with fat stranding in the tail of the pancreas and elevated lipase. His pain improved with NPO status, IV fluids, and analgesia. He was transitioned to a clear diet, then advanced to soft foods, and managed his diabetes with adjusted insulin dosing. He remained stable, with improving labs, and was discharged home with instructions to avoid fatty foods, monitor weight, and continue all home medications including a short course of oral hydromorphone for pain.
